ai.title: CLI release version 1.0.635
ai.summary: The Freebuff CLI `release/package.json` version was bumped from 1.0.634 to 1.0.635 in this release commit. The change is limited to package metadata; no source, functional, or API changes are included. Shipped user-visible items in 1.0.635 since 1.0.634 include the login page styling refresh, the `/b/:hash` redirect to `go.trybeluga.ai`, the conversation-review scope added to the CLI review screen, Free Mode rate-limit increases, and the Freebuff CLI login flow now targeting `freebuff.com` instead of `codebuff.com`. Notably, evalbuff was reworked to support commit-learning and parallel-agent modes with trace compression for documentation optimization.
ai.evidence: Modified file `cli/release/package.json` hunk changes the `version` field from `1.0.634` to `1.0.635`. The commit is marked as `release-bump` with stat `+1 / -1`, and no other source files are touched.

eli5.text: This release sharpens up the Freebuff command-line experience with smoother login, fresh onboarding visuals, and more generous free-tier rate limits. Free users get their request ceiling lifted (from 20 per minute to 25, and from 2,000 to 2,500 every five hours, plus daily and weekly caps doubled to 20,000), so bursts of work are less likely to trip a wall. The login flow now routes through freebuff.com for Freebuff builds, and the web sign-in pages got a styling refresh with glassy cards and gradient backgrounds, plus a subtle darkening on button hover for clearer feedback. A new conversation-scope option is available on the review screen so you can ask Freebuff to review only the work completed during the current chat instead of the whole project. The command-line renderer now activates the terminal's alternate screen buffer for cleaner output handling and proper cleanup when it exits. Finally, the team split up the sprawling knowledge docs into focused AGENTS.md and docs/ topics (environment, testing, development agents) and expanded the evalbuff subsystem so automated documentation tuning can walk git history, spawn parallel agents, and compress traces for faster, leaner results. Upgrading gives you higher free usage limits, a cleaner terminal session lifecycle, and quicker, more targeted answers when you ask Freebuff to review just what you changed in the current conversation.

eli5.text: Freebuff CLI 0.0.24 brings several user-facing upgrades that make the tool smoother, more capable, and easier on the eyes. The biggest addition is a new review option that lets you generate a summary of all changes made in your current conversation, so you can quickly see everything you and the AI have edited together. Signing in and logging in now point to the freebuff.com website (for Freebuff builds), keeping your account flow consistent with the latest branding. The login page got a visual refresh with modern gradients and glass-style cards, plus a subtle darkening effect when you hover over the sign-in button. Free users also get higher usage limits, so the free tier lets you make more requests per minute and per day before hitting caps. Finally, an experimental evaluation system called evalbuff was reworked to learn from your project's git history and run multiple AI agents in parallel, helping improve how well the tool understands and edits code over time.

eli5.text: If you log in to the Freebuff web app using your GitHub account, the app will now prefer your Freebuff-specific GitHub credentials when they're provided, and fall back to the existing Codebuff credentials otherwise. The login configuration now accepts these new credentials and automatically picks the right one depending on whether it's running on your local machine or being deployed. You won't notice anything different unless you're setting up a Freebuff-specific GitHub integration, in which case the app will use that connection instead of the default one.

ai.title: evalbuff signal quality fixes and doc writer edit history
ai.summary: commit-task-generator.ts filters lockfile noise (bun.lock, package-lock.json, etc.) from diffs and file lists to improve eval signal quality. docs-optimizer.ts adds DocEditHistoryEntry interface and formatEditHistory function to track accepted/rejected doc edits with score deltas, feeding history into the analysis prompt. run-evalbuff.ts commits pre-loaded docs into test repos to prevent git diff HEAD corruption, adds scoreBefore/scoreAfter to docsKept/docsRejected arrays, and caps improvement iterations at 5.

eli5.text: When the system grades coding assistants by comparing their edits to real commits, it now ignores automatically generated files like lockfiles so the grade reflects the assistant's own work instead of noise. The grading also tracks each attempted documentation improvement, including the before and after scores, and only counts an edit as a real improvement when it lifts the score by at least 0.3 points, then stops after five rounds of trying. If you were reviewing these results you'd see cleaner before/after comparisons and fewer edits that look helpful only because of file noise.
